issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette: Sameer was twenty-two when the mortar round shattered his world. He had been unloading crates in a makeshift market when the earth bucked beneath his boots, and the initial blast ripped the air before a cascade of concussive bangs vibrated through his chest. What frightened him most was the suffocating lack of control as dust choked his lungs and the ground turned to rubble. In that suspended moment, the smell of cordite and burning rubber clung to his clothes, while the sudden violence of the explosion sounds convinced him that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore and that the world was a dangerous place. Those appraisals did not stay abstract. Every time he caught that phantom scent of smoke on a city street or heard a car backfire, the olfactory and auditory triggers instantly pulled the traumatic memory into sharp relief, dragging him back to the market. His body would lock into the exact crouch he had held while crawling over shattered concrete, and the overwhelming grief of losing his comrades rose in his chest until it felt impossible to draw air. Because the story of that day felt so extreme that it was hard to believe it actually happened to him, he told himself he had fractured beyond repair. As weeks stretched into months, this cycle calcified into a rigid routine. His belief that the world was a dangerous place left him perpetually scanning his environment, which magnified ordinary smells and sudden bangs into severe triggers. His hypervigilance—being superalert and watchful—ensured that his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, which in turn kept his threat system primed for the next trigger. This relentless alertness fed the memories, making him startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, while the resulting flashbacks immediately deepened his conviction that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. Feeling trapped in a dangerous world with a body that never rested, he adopted a new routine. To outrun the paralyzing sense of lost meaning and the crushing grief on recall, he worked hard at keeping busy with other things, scrubbing surfaces and driving himself through double shifts, while strictly avoiding news reports about events similar to what happened to him. Yet this busyness did not silence the storm. His rumination about why the event happened to him left him mentally looping over the past, which inadvertently heightened his sensitivity to triggers and kept his threat responses active. Each avoided headline and each frantic work session maintained his state of tension, ensuring that when a memory did surface, his body on alert would flare instantly, deepening his conviction that he was no longer capable. The more he tried to stay occupied and avoid the news, the more his maladaptive strategies inadvertently primed his nervous system, causing the traumatic memories to break through with greater intensity. Now fifty-three, Sameer spends his days restoring murals in a historic community center, but the trade has become a minefield. Standing on scaffolding to match pigments, he is hyper-vigilant and watchful, his eyes darting to the street below where delivery doors slam with sudden explosion sounds that make him jump at ordinary noises. He knows he cannot sustain this pace. He finally came to the clinic because his wife found him pacing the driveway at 3 a.m., breathless and convinced he smelled burning rubber, while he sat with her at the kitchen table admitting he was terrified the grief would swallow him whole if he stopped running. What he hopes for is a quiet mind; what he fears is that stepping onto a ladder will be the moment everything collapses again, pulling him back to the exact position he held on that shattered street.
